question: Can bounded target-to-behavior stationary occupancy restore parametric accuracy when evaluating a policy’s long-run reward from one partially observed behavior trajectory? Current-action weighting changes today’s action distribution but leaves today’s state distributed according to earlier behavior actions. Weighting longer action histories addresses that accumulated effect, at an increasing variance cost.
result: The estimand is θ(K,e)=Σ_s d_e(s)Σ_a e(a|x)E_K[Y_t|S_t=s,A_t=a]. Under finite observed and hidden state spaces, binary actions, known policies depending only on observed state, sequentially ignorable behavior randomization, a stationary behavior start, |Y_t|≤1, action overlap e(a|x)≤Lb(a|x), contraction by α under both policies, and stationary overlap d_e(s)≤Cd_b(s), the observable minimax mean squared error satisfies c_lo r_T≤R_T≤c_hi r_T, where r_T=T^−1+T^−β q_C^{2(1−β)}, β=2/(2+t_0ζ), q_C=(C−1)/C, L=exp(ζ), and α=exp(−1/t_0). For fixed positive t_0 and ζ, the constants and sufficiently-large-T threshold depend only on those parameters, uniformly over C≥1 and finite state counts. The proposed estimator uses supplied bounds t_0, ζ, and C. Fixed C>1 gives the slower T^−β rate; q_C of order T^−1/2 or smaller permits T^−1 mean squared error.
mechanism: For each reward, multiply the target-to-behavior action ratios over the current action and k previous actions: Z_t(k)=Y_t∏_{j=t−k}^t[e(A_j|X_j)/b(A_j|X_j)]. Average complete windows and clip the estimate to [−1,1]. Sequential ignorability makes the population score equal to Σ_s d_b(s)(P_e^k g_e)(s): the window runs target transitions from a behavior-distributed starting state. Stationary overlap bounds the initial distribution mismatch by q_C, and k target transitions shrink it to the scale q_Cα^k. Squared bias therefore has scale q_C²α^{2k}, while variance has scale L^k/T, with an additional ordinary sampling term. Use k=0 when Tq_C²≤1; otherwise choose the integer depth near log(Tq_C²)/[2log(1/α)+log L], capped at T/2. This balance gives the upper risk bound. For the lower bound, construct two hidden depth-and-sign models with opposite reward responses at terminal depth Q. Their target values differ, but observed rewards reveal that difference only through surviving sign memory and a rare terminal state. Choose Q so the observed trajectory laws remain hard to distinguish while their target-value separation matches the upper-bound rate.
why_true: The occupancy restriction supplies a quantitative starting-bias bound, even though the full state is hidden. Mixing then repairs that bias through observable history weights. Conditional mean-one action ratios and mixing control window covariance, so overlapping windows do not impose an extra factor of history length. The lower construction explains why another observable estimator cannot generally escape the tradeoff: terminal probability remains bounded by K_0α^Q even after conditioning on favorable reward histories. Because terminal depth is hidden, that probability enters the observed reward mean before distinguishability squares it. Consequently KL is bounded by a constant times Tε_C²α^{2Q}L^−Q, whereas squared target-value separation has scale ε_C²α^{2Q}. Since q_C/2≤ε_C≤q_C, balancing these quantities reproduces the same exponent and radius dependence. Ordinary reward uncertainty supplies the T^−1 floor.
example: The observed state is constant, while hidden state records depth J and sign U. Advances occur with probability α until terminal depth Q; resets draw a sign with mean ε_C. The target always chooses action one and preserves sign during advances. Behavior chooses action one with probability 1/L; action zero redraws sign fairly. Thus both policies have stationary depth mass w_j=(1−α)α^j/(1−α^{Q+1}), but their conditional sign means are ε_C under target and ε_CL^−j under behavior. With opposite reward responses v=±1 only at terminal depth, target value is v c_0 ε_C w_Q. All-one histories receive positive importance weight and reproduce target sign preservation. Increasing Q makes those histories and terminal rewards difficult to observe while maintaining the occupancy restriction.
